Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy
Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
Being reminded of the event by others

Threat.value: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Negative Appraisals.value: The world is a dangerous place
I have to be on guard all the time
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened
issues.explanation: The appraisal of permanent bodily damage is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile and trauma context. The other selected items consistently reflect ongoing external danger and hyperarousal (world dangerous, on guard, startle, false alarms, threat in silence) plus intrusive sensory memory, but there are no corroborating memory, threat, or strategy items indicating injury-focused trauma consequences, pain, disability, or body-related threat. For a refugee trauma profile, this isolated somatic-damage belief is not impossible, but in this item set it stands out as clinically incoherent with the dominant formulation of danger-based threat and avoidance.

vignette: Max, a 21-year-old male of European descent, is a public defender in his early career. Max fled his home country at age 18 after experiencing traumatic events that have left deep emotional scars. His journey to America was fraught with peril and fear, leaving him feeling vulnerable and exposed. The intensity of the experiences he endured has led to significant psychological distress. Max’s trauma began during a particularly volatile period in his homeland, where political unrest and violence were rampant. One night, while fleeing from a violent mob, Max found himself trapped in an alleyway with no escape route. The sounds of shattering glass and shouted threats filled the air around him as he huddled against a wall, trying to remain unseen. Despite the silence that eventually settled, Max was certain something dangerous was still lurking nearby, waiting to strike. Since then, Max has been plagued by vivid visual memories of that night. When these images surface, his body feels as if it is reenacting those moments in the alleyway—his heart races, and he relives the terror and fear. Sometimes, even without a clear image, the emotional intensity hits him with full force, leaving him feeling raw and vulnerable. Max has come to believe that the world is an inherently dangerous place, a conviction reinforced by his constant vigilance and fear of what might happen next. This belief drives him to monitor his own thoughts constantly for signs of going crazy and to avoid talking about the traumatic event or its aftermath with others, as he fears these discussions will trigger overwhelming emotional responses. His heightened sense of threat is evident in how he reacts to ordinary sounds—jumps at unexpected noises—and feels on edge when there’s unusual silence. These reactions often lead him to believe that he must be extra careful and hyper-aware, further entrenching his negative appraisals about the world's danger. Max’s occupation as a public defender exacerbates these symptoms. The courtroom environment, with its unpredictable nature and constant reminders of violence and injustice, triggers his memories and heightens his sense of threat. His aversion to discussing his past experiences with colleagues makes it difficult for him to build supportive relationships at work, leading to feelings of isolation and further reinforcing his belief that he cannot trust others. The cycle begins when Max’s vivid memories surface, causing a surge in anxiety and physical reenactment. This triggers his heightened sense of threat, making him jump at every sound and react as if danger is imminent. These reactions lead him to monitor his thoughts more closely and avoid talking about the event, further isolating himself. Max’s constant vigilance has also strained his relationship with his partner. He often avoids going out together or attending social gatherings due to fears of being reminded of his traumatic experiences. This avoidance has led to misunderstandings and arguments, deepening his sense that he is alone in dealing with his trauma. What finally brought Max to seek help was a particularly severe episode during a trial where the sound of a door slamming triggered a full-blown panic attack. He realized that his ability to perform his job effectively was at stake, and he was afraid of losing both his career and his relationship. Despite these fears, Max is hoping for relief from the constant vigilance and the ability to trust others again without feeling overwhelmed by memories and threats. Max’s story illustrates a self-reinforcing cycle where his negative appraisals about the world's danger drive his maladaptive strategies and heighten his threat responses, which in turn reinforce his negative beliefs. The vicious loop is evident in how each component feeds into the next, creating an ongoing state of heightened anxiety and isolation.
